summary.text: A flower is the reproductive structure of a flowering plant, typically built in four circular levels around the end of a stalk.
Sepals support the flower, petals often attract pollinators, stamens present pollen, and the female gynoecia receive it.
After pollination and fertilisation, the resulting cell grows into a seed while the female part of the flower forms a fruit and the other floral structures die.

facts.label: Cone equivalent
facts.value: Cones are the gymnosperm counterpart of flowers

items.prompt: A bee lands on a flower and gets dusted with pollen from the tip of a slender organ. Which part presented that pollen?

options.label: The female gynoecia
The male stamens
The supporting sepals
The showy petals

items.explain: Stamens are the male parts where pollen is presented; gynoecia are the female parts that receive it.

items.prompt: A plant relies on insects to carry its pollen. Why would it have brightly coloured petals?

options.label: Their colour and form help draw pollinators in
They hold the egg cell safe inside the flower
They support the whole flower on its stalk
They grow into the fruit after pollination

items.explain: Petals are often designed to attract pollinators, and the colour and structure of flowers assist pollination.

items.prompt: Why do plants tend to favour cross-pollination over self-pollination?

options.label: It lets the flower skip fertilisation altogether
It keeps every offspring identical to its parent
It makes the fruit ripen much more quickly
It joins sex cells from different plants, adding diversity

items.explain: Cross-pollination brings together sex cells from genetically distinct plants of the same species, which increases genetic diversity.

items.prompt: A flower has just been pollinated and fertilised. What soon happens to its female part?

options.label: It grows into a fresh bud on the same stalk
It dies back along with the other floral structures
It forms a fruit while the other floral structures die
It turns into a sepal that wraps the seed

items.explain: After fertilisation the female part of the flower forms a fruit, and the other floral structures die.

items.prompt: A bird eats a fruit and drops the seeds later in a faraway spot. What job of the fruit does this show?

options.label: Carrying pollen between separate flowers
Guarding the seed and spreading it away from the parent
Turning pollen into a seed
Feeding the embryo before it is fertilised

items.explain: The function of fruit is to protect the seed and aid in its dispersal, and living things such as birds can spread the seeds.

items.prompt: Flowering plants replaced non-flowering plants in many ecosystems. What explains this?

options.label: They evolved before any other kind of plant
They grew far larger than non-flowering plants
They no longer needed pollination to make seeds
Flowers made them more effective at reproducing

items.explain: Plants with flowers replaced non-flowering plants in many ecosystems as a result of flowers' superior reproductive effectiveness.

paragraphs.heading: What a flower is
paragraphs.text: A flower, also called a blossom or bloom, is the reproductive structure of a flowering plant, or angiosperm. Cones play the matching role in gymnosperms. The main job of a flower is to reproduce the plant, which helps the species survive. When several flowers are grouped together, the cluster is called an inflorescence.

paragraphs.heading: Four rings of parts
paragraphs.text: A typical flower is built in four rings, called whorls, around the tip of a short stalk. The thickened top of that stalk, the receptacle, holds up everything else. From the base upward, the whorls are the calyx, the petals, the androecium and the gynoecium. The calyx is made of sepals, modified leaves on the outermost ring that support the flower, and with the petals it forms the perianth, the part that plays no role in reproduction. Petals often attract pollinators, the male stamens present pollen, and the female gynoecium receives pollen and helps it reach the egg.

paragraphs.heading: Moving the pollen
paragraphs.text: Most flowers can make sex cells of both sexes. Pollen, which can produce the male sex cells, has to move between male and female parts, and this is called pollination. It can happen between different plants, known as cross-pollination, or within one plant or even one flower, known as self-pollination. Animals such as birds and insects carry pollen, and so do wind and water, while a flower's colour and structure help the process along. Plants favour cross-pollination because joining sex cells from genetically distinct plants of one species raises genetic diversity, and features that draw pollinators are among the most common adaptations.

paragraphs.heading: From flower to seed
paragraphs.text: After pollination, the sex cells fuse in fertilisation. The resulting cell divides and grows into a seed, which holds an embryo and usually a food reserve inside a protective coat. Meanwhile the female part of the flower becomes a fruit and the other floral parts die. The fruit protects the seed and helps carry it away from the parent, whether in the droppings of birds that eat it or by wind and water.

paragraphs.heading: A long history
paragraphs.text: The first flowers appeared in the Jurassic, between 150 and 190 million years ago. Because they reproduce more effectively, flowering plants replaced non-flowering ones in many ecosystems, and today they dominate most of the world's ecosystems, from tiny orchids and crops to large trees. Their size, shape, colour and smell vary enormously. Flowers range in size from 0.1 mm to 1 metre.

paragraphs.heading: Flowers and people
paragraphs.text: Botanists rely on flowers as a key feature for telling plants apart. People have used them for thousands of years for decoration, medicine, food and perfume, and as symbols in art, literature, religion and festivals. The word reached Middle English through Old French from the Latin flōs. Until the 17th century it was often spelled flour, a spelling that then came to mean ground grain, from the figurative sense of the finest part.
